chapter: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
title: Writing for Bobby Lippert's band in Detroit
summary: He wrote for a white Detroit band as an experiment, drafting 'McGhee Special' and 'Paradise Valley'.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. Well, I was writing for a White band in Detroit named Bobby Lippert.
When you ended up in Detroit after the tour of the territories.
Yeah, right. This was after I come through the New Mexico and Canada...

Yeah. So I was in Detroit. I was working with a small band, and he had a bigger band, and he wanted some music. So I knew how to write the tunes that he wanted. I could always get a piano sheet and write out how I wanted it to sound. And he loved it, because he used to... You know, he'd come by my house every day, and 'You got something new for me to play?'...

Oh, he had about five brass and five reeds and four rhythm. Bobby Lippert. He was very nice. In fact, he used to spend a lot of money with me just because I would write for him, and I would try and write what he wanted.
Yeah, about 1940 or '41. Yeah. This is when I was learning how to scribble for myself, too, you know -- by using his band as an experimental band. I was

able to write... So when they formed the band for the Commodore Club, all they had to do was just damn near take my scores out and copy them over, and give them to the guys. So it saved me a lot of work. Because it's a bitch to try to sit up there and write a whole new book for a band without repeating yourself, and that's definitely...

Like, I had some original tunes already, like "McGhee Special" and "Paradise Valley" and some things that I had really sketched out for Bobby's band, and I just took them and put my stuff to them, and changed them around a little bit more when I recorded them with Andy's band. But it was a nice thing to know that I could do that. Because I mean, it ain't every day that you can (?) somebody that knows how to write, whether they good or they write bad -- but still, if they don't know how to write, it's a drag.
